q: what happens inside a black hole
what happens when you enter a black hole
what happens at the singularity of a black hole
a: Falling into a black hole would subject you to extreme physical phenomena. As you approach the event horizon (the point of no return), you would experience spaghettification, where the enormous tidal forces stretch your body into a long, thin strand because the gravitational pull on the part of your body closest to the black hole is vastly stronger than on the farthest part. For a stellar-mass black hole, spaghettification occurs before you reach the event horizon. For a supermassive black hole, you could cross the event horizon without being torn apart because the tidal forces at the horizon are much weaker. After crossing the event horizon, there is no possible path that leads back out. Inside the black hole, all paths lead toward the singularity, a point of infinite density and zero volume where the laws of physics as we know them break down. General relativity predicts that at the singularity, spacetime curvature becomes infinite, and matter is crushed to an infinitely small point. Time dilation becomes extreme: to a distant observer, you appear to slow down and freeze at the event horizon, never quite crossing it, while you would experience crossing it normally. The interior of a black hole is causally disconnected from the rest of the universe, meaning no information about what happens inside can ever escape. Hawking radiation suggests that black holes slowly evaporate over immense timescales, but what happens to the information that fell in remains one of the biggest unsolved problems in physics (the information paradox).
